content: On August 15, 1988, a program advisory committee on the human genome was established to provide guidance to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) on all aspects of genomic research. On October 1, 1988, the Office for Human Genome Research was created within the NIH Office of the Director. On the same day, the NIH and the Department of Energy (DOE) signed a memorandum of understanding to coordinate research and technical activities related to the human genome. On January 3-4, 1989, the program advisory committee on the human genome held its first meeting in Bethesda, Maryland. On October 1, 1989, the National Center for Human Genome Research (NCHGR) was established to oversee the NIH's component of the U.S. Human Genome Project. James D. Watson, co-discoverer of the DNA double helix, was appointed as the center's first director. In April 1990, a five-year plan with specific goals for the Human Genome Project was published. On May 8, 1990, the National Advisory Council for Human Genome Research was established. On July 1, 1990, the Genome Research Review Committee was created to ensure proper peer review of human genome grant applications by the NCHGR. On October 1, 1990, the Human Genome Project officially began. On January 22, 1991, the National Advisory Council for Human Genome Research held its first meeting in Bethesda, Maryland. On April 10, 1992, James Watson resigned as the first director of the NCHGR, and Michael Gottesman was appointed as acting director. In February 1993, the Division of Intramural Research (DIR) was established within the NCHGR. On April 4, 1993, Francis S. Collins was appointed as the director of the NCHGR. On October 1, 1993, the U.S. Human Genome Project revised its five-year goals, extending them through September 1998. On September 30, 1994, the goal of human genetic mapping was achieved one year ahead of schedule. On November 15, 1995, the NCHGR celebrated its fifth anniversary and established the James D. Watson Lecture. In April 1995, the Task Force on Genetic Testing was created as a subgroup of the NIH/DOE Ethical, Legal, and Social Implications (ELSI) Working Group. On April 11, 1996, human DNA sequencing began with pilot studies at six U.S. universities. On April 24, 1996, an international team completed the DNA sequence of the first eukaryotic genome, Saccharomyces cerevisiae (brewer's yeast). In September 1996, the Center for Inherited Disease Research (CIDR) was established at the Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center campus in Baltimore to study the genetic components of complex disorders. In October 1996, scientists worldwide revealed a map pinpointing the locations of over 16,000 genes in human DNA. In November 1996, researchers identified the location of the first gene associated with Parkinson's disease and the first major gene predisposing men to prostate cancer. In December 1996, the ELSI Report was issued by the NIH/DOE Joint Committee, evaluating the ethical, legal, and social implications of the Human Genome Project. In January 1997, the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Secretary Donna E. Shalala renamed the NCHGR as the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), reflecting its growth and accomplishments. In March 1997, a government-citizen group proposed policies to limit genetic discrimination in the workplace. In May 1997, NHGRI scientists demonstrated that specific alterations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes are associated with increased risks of breast, ovarian, and prostate cancers. In June 1997, NHGRI scientists identified a gene abnormality causing some cases of Parkinson's disease. In July 1997, a map of human chromosome 7 was completed. In August 1997, the NHGRI Office of Science Education launched its first Genomics Short Course for college teachers at NIH. In December 1997, NHGRI researchers identified an altered gene causing Pendred Syndrome, an inherited form of deafness. In March 1998, Vice President Al Gore announced the Clinton administration's call for legislation to prevent genetic discrimination in hiring or promotion. In September 1998, Human Genome Project planners presented a new plan to produce a finished version of the human genome sequence by 2003, two years ahead of schedule, with a working draft available by 2001. In September 1998, an international study identified a gene for prostate cancer susceptibility on the X chromosome, marking the first time a common cancer gene was mapped to the X chromosome. In October 1998, the NIH and DOE published a new five-year plan for the Human Genome Project, covering fiscal years 1999 through 2003. In December 1998, researchers sequenced the genome of the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. In March 1999, large-scale sequencing of the human genome began. In September 1999, Human Genome Project scientists confirmed they were on schedule to produce a working draft of the human genome by spring 2000. In October 1999, President Clinton and First Lady Hillary Clinton hosted the eighth Millennium Evening at the White House, titled Informatics Meets Genomics. On November 12, 1999, NHGRI hosted its first annual Consumer Day conference to inform patients, families, and healthcare providers about the Human Genome Project's impact. In December 1999, NHGRI and other researchers unraveled the genetic code of an entire human chromosome for the first time. In February 2000, President Clinton signed an executive order to prevent genetic discrimination in federal workplaces. In March 2000, a public-private consortium released a substantially complete genome sequence of the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster). In April 2000, NHGRI co-sponsored the first NIH Conference on Holoprosencephaly. In May 2000, scientists in Japan and Germany sequenced human chromosome 21, associated with Down syndrome, Alzheimer's disease, and other conditions. In June 2000, the Human Genome Project consortium announced it had assembled 85% of the human genome sequence. In August 2000, scientists discovered a genetic signature explaining how malignant melanoma spreads. In October 2000, the Mouse Genome Sequencing Consortium was formed to accelerate the sequencing of the mouse genome. In February 2001, the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium published the first analysis of the human genome sequence, revealing there are only 30,000 to 40,000 genes, far fewer than previously thought. In March 2001, NHGRI researchers identified a new tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 7 involved in various cancers. In May 2001, the Mouse Genome Sequencing Consortium achieved three-fold coverage of the mouse genome sequence. In September 2001, NHGRI announced the first Centers of Excellence in Genomic Science (CEGS) awards. In October 2003, NHGRI announced the first grants for the ENCODE project, aimed at identifying all functional elements in the human genome. In April 2003, NHGRI celebrated the completion of the human genome sequence and the 50th anniversary of the DNA double helix discovery. In October 2004, NHGRI announced the first draft of the chimpanzee genome sequence.
